name: Archetype: Soviet-model armies (Warsaw Pact and clients, 1945-91)

weightNotes.aggression: FM 100-2-1 (1984): Soviet doctrine is offensive, aiming to seize the initiative at the outset of hostilities and carry the war onto enemy territory; defence is a temporary phase.
weightNotes.maneuver: Deep operation and the operational maneuver group (OMG) aim at tempo and depth (FM 100-2-1 ch. 4; CIA 1983 OMG assessment), but by massing on narrow breakthrough sectors with heavy artillery. A mix of mass and manoeuvre, so 0.6.
weightNotes.flanking: Doctrine prefers bypassing strongpoints, envelopment and exploitation into the rear by mobile groups and air assault; tactically, attacks still went in on norm-prescribed narrow frontages. Middling-high.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Cities are bypassed and left to second echelons; advance norms of up to about 30-50 km a day (FM 100-2-1) leave no time for sieges. Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: FM 100-2-1: second echelons were as much as half of an attacking formation (two divisions of a four-division army) when facing deep defences, plus combined-arms and special reserves; lighter when the defender was thin.
weightNotes.scouting: Dedicated reconnaissance units at every echelon, Spetsnaz and the reconnaissance-strike complex concept; middling because tactical intelligence fusion was slow and rigid.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.coldwar high quartile 0.154. Sourced refusal to withdraw: echelons were expected to fight until exhausted and then be passed through by the next echelon rather than fall back (FM 100-2-1, 1984). No measured share; previous 0.3 was a judgment above the era's whole loser range. Kept under the evidence rule (QA round 4): echelon doctrine fixes when a committed formation stops (fight until exhausted, then be passed through), a tactical holding norm, not caution about attacking.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Combined arms combat is the core of Soviet doctrine (FM 100-2-1): tank, motor rifle, artillery, air defence, engineers and frontal aviation integrated by norm. Below the Western profile because coordination was rigid and pre-planned.
weightNotes.initiative: FM 100-2-1, 'Norms, initiative and flexibility': a given situation has an approved normative response; 'probably little tactical flexibility at subunit level (battalion and lower)'; flexibility grows with rank.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Norms prescribe supply rates and a push-forward system, but the offensive design accepts outrunning supply for the sake of tempo. Middling.

summary: Massive mechanised armies built on the Soviet model: tank and motor rifle divisions, very large artillery parks and integrated air defence, fighting by mathematical norms. The offensive seeks a breakthrough on a narrow sector with crushing artillery density (FM 100-2-1 cites 60-100 tubes per km on a main attack), followed by second echelons and operational maneuver groups exploiting deep into the enemy rear at high tempo. Command is centralised; junior commanders execute drills. Cadre divisions fill out by mass mobilisation of reservists.
whyItWorked: Mass, tempo and simplicity: norms and drills let a conscript army execute complex operations, and echeloning sustained the momentum of an offensive in a way NATO planners feared enough to rewrite their doctrine (AirLand Battle and Follow-on Forces Attack). It crushed Hungary 1956 and Czechoslovakia 1968 quickly and North Korea's 1950 offensive nearly overran the South.
whereItFailed: Afghanistan 1979-1989: a force designed for European mechanised war struggled against dispersed mujahideen in mountains and had to improvise with air assault and small-unit tactics (Grau, The Bear Went Over the Mountain). Client armies with Soviet kit and doctrine but less training were routed by Western-model forces: Egypt and Syria 1967 and 1973 (after the Canal crossing), Iraq 1991. Rigidity left units helpless when the plan broke.
